english: the merchant fearing, leisure and of his town
problem: 'his' renders sui, which stands on line 17 (and is rendered again there), so a word is carried over from the next line.
suggested: the merchant, fearing, leisure and of the town

latin: multos castra iuvant et lituo tubae
english: Many the camps delight, and with the lituus of the trumpet
problem: tubae is genitive with sonitus (line 24), 'the sound of the trumpet mingled with the lituus', not a genitive dependent on lituo.
suggested: Many the camps delight, and, with the lituus, of the trumpet

english: right hand having struck the sacred citadels
problem: iaculatus means 'having hurled (bolts) at', not 'having struck'; the note gives the literal sense but the line does not.
suggested: right hand having hurled at the sacred citadels

english: by which the grievous Persians had better perished,
problem: 'had better perished' is ungrammatical and blurs the imperfect subjunctive perirent; the note's own 'would better perish/have perished' is the literal sense.
suggested: by which the grievous Persians would better perish,

english: Whom of the gods should the people call to the of a falling
problem: 'to the' is the dative of rebus on line 26, so its English is moved onto this line, leaving line 26 without it.
suggested: Whom of the gods should the people call, of a falling

english: So may you the goddess powerful over Cyprus,
problem: 'may' is the mood of regat on line 3, moved onto line 1; line 3 then renders regat without it.
suggested: So you the goddess powerful over Cyprus,

problem: Leti is genitive (the necessity of Death, from line 32); 'Death' is rendered as the subject of corripuit, changing the sense.

latin: iam te premet nox fabulaeque Manes
english: soon will press upon you night and the fabled Manes
problem: The note takes fabulae as a nominative noun in apposition ('stories'), but the line renders it as the adjective 'fabled'.
suggested: soon will press upon you night and the Manes, tales,
